candidates.title: Endophytic fungi shape tree epigenomes and enhance thermotolerance under climate warming.
candidates.abstract: Rising global temperatures threaten the survival and regeneration of temperate and boreal forests. Yet how microbial symbioses contribute to tree heat-resilience remains unclear. Here, we integrated field ecological surveys with controlled multi-omics analyses and found that soil fungal diversity declined, accompanied by enrichment of potentially beneficial taxa along regional variation in max temperature of the warmest month (BIO5). Inoculation with representative endophytes significantly promoted birch (Betula platyphylla) growth and photosynthetic performance under non-stress conditions. Furthermore, endophytic fungi enhance thermal tolerance in birch by establishing a transcriptional chromatin state at heat-responsive genes that facilitates their activation under heat stress. Integrative network analyses identified regulatory networks linking fungal symbiosis to thermotolerance pathways. These findings connect macroecological patterns to molecular mechanisms, uncovering an epigenetic basis for microbe-mediated heat adaptation in trees and highlighting symbiotic fungi as both key partners and practical means to strengthen forest resilience under climate warming. candidates.title: Temperature-sensitive N6-methyladenosine interactions prime the malaria parasite for transmission
candidates.abstract: Abstract To infect a mosquito vector, malaria parasites differentiate into male and female semi-quiescent gametocytes that can re-initiate development within seconds after transmission. The rapid switch from gametocytes to gametes relies on multiple environmental changes, yet the molecular events driving this developmental transition remain unclear. Here, using high-resolution RNA and ribosome profiling, we identify the mRNA modification N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) as an essential mechanism to restructure protein synthesis during Plasmodium falciparum transmission. We show that male parasites rapidly repress translation of m 6 A-methylated transcripts after mosquito uptake via the binding of YTH.2, a reader protein with an m 6 A-binding domain. This repressive interaction is temperature sensitive and requires the temperature drop accompanying human-to-mosquito transmission. Hence, m 6 A primes the transcriptome during semi-quiescence for a post-transcriptional response that is activated by an environmental shift. These data reveal how unicellular organisms incorporate external stimuli for lifecycle progression, providing potential avenues to combat malaria.

candidates.title: Debudding uncouples the phenology of xylogenesis in Abies georgei var. smithii
candidates.abstract: Abstract Investigating radial growth dynamics is crucial for understanding climate-growth relationships in alpine treeline, where the linkage between primary and secondary growth remains contentious. To clarify the influence of apical growth on stem growth in treeline trees, we conducted a debudding experiment on Abies georgei var. smithii in the Jiaozi Snow Mountain National Nature Reserve in Yunnan, before the 2023 growing season, while no interventions were performed to allow natural recovery in 2024. During the study, the radial growth dynamics of the stems and shoots were monitored weekly, and the xylem anatomical traits (i.e., lumen radial diameter and cell wall thickness) were quantified along cell radial files after the xylem lignification was completed. We demonstrated that debudding advanced the onset of growth in stems and shoots compared with the control group, while also increasing shoot cell number and the rate of cell wall deposition. Furthermore, it amplified the influence of photoperiod on stem growth rate without altering the approximately 5°C threshold for radial growth initiation. Our findings clarify the critical role of apical meristems in regulating xylogenesis in treeline trees and provide novel insights into the intrinsic coordination between primary and secondary growth, which is significant for understanding the growth adaptive strategies of treeline trees in the future climate.

candidates.title: Establishment of a Tobacco Rattle Virus-Mediated Virus-Induced Gene Silencing System in Eucommia ulmoides
candidates.abstract: A virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) system would allow rapid functional testing of genes in Eucommia ulmoides, but no such system has been reported for this species. We used phytoene desaturase (EuPDS) as a reporter and delivered a silencing construct into cotyledons by Agrobacterium-mediated infiltration. Mottled chlorosis appeared on newly developed true leaves about 28 days after injection, when cotyledons were infiltrated at the onset of true-leaf emergence. Reverse-transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) showed a strong reduction in EuPDS transcripts in the chlorotic tissue, confirming systemic silencing. Optimisation of the infiltration parameters showed that silencing was most efficient with a bacterial suspension of OD600 = 0.6 and 200 μM acetosyringone (AS). A fragment from the EuPDS-N region also outperformed EuPDS-M. The optimised system silenced EuPDS in the cultivars ‘Huazhong 10’ and ‘Huazhong 30’ as well, which suggests that it is not restricted to a single genetic background. This method does not require tissue-culture-based plant regeneration and provides a practical route to the functional characterisation of genes underlying rubber biosynthesis, secondary metabolism and stress responses in E. ulmoides.

candidates.title: Metatranscriptomic Characterization of the Virome Associated with Globally Distributed Phlebotomine Sandflies
candidates.abstract: Phlebotomine sandflies are hematophagous vectors of major medical and veterinary significance, yet their resident virome remains largely unexplored. Characterizing these viral communities is crucial to understanding vector ecology and its impact on animal and agricultural health. In this exploratory survey, we investigated viral diversity across New and Old-World lineages by mining 162 public RNA-sequencing libraries from 15 sandfly species using a validated transcriptomic pipeline. Our analysis recovered 47 non-redundant putative viral sequences representing 35 viruses across 16 families. A divergent tombus-like lineage was the most widely distributed group among Old World Phlebotomus species, alongside viruses whose characterized relatives infect plants and fungi. Notably, in the non-vector species Sergentomyia schwetzi, we recovered the two most completely assembled genomes of the survey, an iflavirus and a dicistrovirus, the first a new species and the second the first species-level record of a virus previously known only from genus-level pools. In the New World, we identified the first record of Polycipiviridae in phlebotomines, alongside a putative nodavirus in Nyssomyia neivai. Most recovered viruses were insect-specific and host-restricted; however, the tombus-like lineage was shared across five Old World Phlebotomus species, indicating that related viruses can circulate among distinct sandfly hosts. Lutzomyia nodavirus was detected at low abundance in embryonic-stage libraries, raising the question of how it is maintained between generations, which remains to be tested experimentally. These findings suggest that sandfly viromes reflect the ecological niches these insects occupy. This work expands the documented viral diversity in these species and highlights the value of publicly available transcriptomic data for continuous environmental surveillance.

candidates.title: From lesions to patients: multi-lesion imaging AI for response and survival prediction in immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy
candidates.abstract: Patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy may exhibit divergent responses across lesions, whereas treatment decisions and clinical outcomes are largely defined at the patient level. Multi-lesion imaging artificial intelligence (AI) offers a means of bridging these scales, but its predictive value depends on how interlesional information is selected, represented, and aggregated. This focused narrative review examines the lesion-to-patient modeling pipeline, drawing on evidence from ICI-treated cohorts while distinguishing related oncology applications and general AI methods. We discuss lesion selection and supervision, organ-aware representation, set aggregation, and longitudinal modeling, with particular attention to the information retained at each stage. Multiple instance learning is distinguished from aggregation architectures, and baseline prediction from models incorporating on-treatment imaging. Within validation, we propose three complementary dimensions: accessibility of prespecified lesion-set properties, incremental patient-level predictive value beyond clinical and tumor-burden baselines, and agreement between explicit lesion predictions and independently observed outcomes. Current studies demonstrate the feasibility of lesion-level modeling and patient-level integration, but have not established consistent benefits from broader lesion sampling or more complex aggregation strategies. Future research should prioritize transparent lesion-selection rules, time-aligned inputs and outcomes, controlled comparisons with simpler models, and external validation of complete pipelines. These efforts are needed to establish when multi-lesion imaging provides clinically meaningful predictive information without conflating prognostic performance with differential treatment benefit.

candidates.title: Genome-Wide Identification and Expression Analysis of LBD Gene Family in Cucumis sativus L.
candidates.abstract: LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN (LBD) transcription factors play pivotal roles in plant growth, development and stress responses. However, their genome-wide characterization and functions in cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.) remain largely unexplored. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive bioinformatic analysis of the CsLBD gene family and investigated its expression patterns under different stresses in cucumber. A total of 41 CsLBD genes were identified and phylogenetically classified into two major classes. The CsLBD genes exhibited an uneven distribution across cucumber chromosomes, and their encoded proteins contain the characteristic conserved domains, specifically including the canonical CX2CX6CX3C zinc finger domain and the LX6LX3LX6L leucine zipper-like motif. Promoter cis-element analysis suggested potential roles for CsLBDs in hormone signaling, stress response, and growth regulation. Tissue-specific expression profiling revealed that several members, including CsLBD19, CsLBD26, and CsLBD30, were highly expressed in tendril, whereas others such as CsLBD12, CsLBD15, and CsLBD27 were preferentially expressed in root, implying their distinct roles in organ development. Crucially, expression analysis under various stresses demonstrated that the CsLBD family was widely involved in responses to both biotic and abiotic stresses. Notably, CsLBD07, CsLBD11, and CsLBD14 were significantly upregulated upon powdery mildew infection; numerous members exhibited substantial expression changes in response to gray mold and heat stress; CsLBD02 and CsLBD17 were specifically induced in a resistant line, suggesting their potential roles in disease resistance. Interestingly, CsLBD02 and CsLBD10 responded to all the stresses tested. Our results provide a systematic overview of the CsLBD gene family and contribute valuable insights towards the further functional characterization of these genes in cucumber growth and stress responses.

candidates.title: Beyond Inhibition: From Growth Arrest to Gene Regulation in Agrobacterium radiobacter Exposed to Monoterpenes
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Monoterpenes, major constituents of essential oils, exhibit broad‐spectrum antimicrobial activity and represent promising candidates for sustainable crop protection. Here, we investigated the responses of the biocontrol bacterium Agrobacterium radiobacter to seven structurally distinct monoterpenes using an integrated approach combining antimicrobial assays, real‐time growth monitoring, matrix‐assisted laser desorption/ionisation time‐of‐flight mass spectrometry (MALDI‐TOF MS) spectral profiling, and gene expression analysis. D‐carvone exhibited the highest antibacterial efficacy (MIC 50 = 0.318 mg/mL), whereas β‐pinene and bornyl acetate were the least active. Real‐time growth monitoring revealed pronounced time‐dependent inhibition, with strong early suppression during the first 0–3 h followed by partial growth recovery. MALDI‐TOF MS analysis demonstrated structure‐specific alterations in bacterial protein spectra, with (S)‐(–)‐limonene and bornyl acetate inducing the most pronounced changes, while β‐pinene and sabinene showed comparatively minor effects. Hierarchical cluster analysis identified 3 h as the most discriminative time point for detecting monoterpene‐induced responses. Gene expression analysis revealed compound‐specific regulation of exoY , hrcS , ftsI , achI and ncpAch , with the strongest transcriptional changes associated with α‐pinene, D‐carvone and 3‐carene. Collectively, discrepancies observed across antimicrobial activity, growth kinetics, protein spectral profiles, and gene expression indicate that monoterpenes do not operate through a single mechanism, but rather elicit multiple, structure‐dependent modes of action. These findings provide mechanistic insight into plant metabolite–rhizosphere bacteria interactions and highlight the importance of integrated approaches for evaluating antimicrobial activity in biological control systems.

candidates.title: Effects of Papenfussiella kuromo Extract on Inflammatory Markers and NF-κB-Associated Proteins in Porphyromonas gingivalis-Stimulated RAW 264.7 Macrophages
candidates.abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by progressive destruction of periodontal supporting tissues resulting from dysregulated host immune responses to periodontal pathogens. Modulation of host inflammatory signaling pathways has thus emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for periodontal disease. In this study, we investigated the anti-inflammatory effects of Papenfussiella kuromo (P. kuromo) extract on Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis)-induced inflammation in RAW 264.7 macrophages. Cell viability was assessed after treatment with the extract alone using an MTS assay; nitric oxide (NO) production was measured by the Griess reaction; inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) expression and NF-κB signaling activation were analyzed by Western blotting; and mRNA levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α) were quantified by qRT-PCR. P. kuromo extract showed no cytotoxicity toward RAW 264.7 macrophages within the selected concentration range. In P. gingivalis-stimulated cells, the extract significantly reduced NO production and suppressed iNOS protein expression. Moreover, P. kuromo extract downregulated IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α mRNA in a concentration-dependent manner. At 24 h, lower IKKα/β and IκBα phosphorylation and reduced nuclear accumulation of NF-κB p65 were also observed. Whether these NF-κB-associated changes contributed to the reductions in inflammatory markers remains to be determined. The relevance of these findings to periodontal disease should be evaluated in future studies using more physiologically relevant models.

candidates.title: The Sec61-EMC complex promotes biosynthesis of the SARS-CoV-2 non-structural proteins
candidates.abstract: The genomic RNA of SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for the global COVID-19 pandemic, encodes polyproteins pp1a and pp1ab which contain 16 non-structural proteins (NSPs) that support critical steps in infection. Despite this, how the polyproteins are synthesized and membrane-inserted in the host cell is unclear. Here we demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 exploits the Sec61-endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane complex (EMC) translation machinery to promote biosynthesis of the virus polyproteins, leading to successful replication and infection. The Sec61-EMC complex engages NSP3—the first transmembrane (TM) protein in pp1a/pp1ab—during active translation. Strikingly, of the four TM segments in NSP3, a marginally hydrophobic domain between TM3 and TM4 is required for EMC-binding and confers EMC-dependent expression. Our results reveal an ER-dependent mechanism for translation of the SARS-CoV-2 NSPs during virus infection, providing insights that should lead to new anti-SARS-CoV-2 therapeutic approaches. Author summary: SARS-CoV-2 viral non-structural proteins (NSPs) are necessary for several key steps of viral infection including double membrane vesicle (DMV) formation, genome replication and transcription, and immune evasion. The NSPs are initially synthesized as one large polyprotein containing several multipass transmembrane proteins that require insertion into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane for productive infection. How the host cell translates and inserts this unique client protein remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that the Sec61-ER membrane complex (EMC) is required for efficient NSP biosynthesis. Mechanistically, we further demonstrate that the marginally hydrophobic domain between transmembrane domains 3 and 4 of NSP3 is the molecular determinant for its EMC dependency.

candidates.title: Time-resolved single-cell phenotyping identifies two major classes of antimicrobial peptides with shared principles and key trade-offs.
candidates.abstract: Cationic antimicrobial peptides are a broad family of host defence molecules that neutralize bacteria by permeabilizing one or more membranes and/or inhibiting intracellular targets. However, the relative timings of these effects and their impact at the population level remain poorly understood. Here we present a time-resolved single-cell pipeline for quantifying these effects in Escherichia coli. Applying this pipeline to 18 diverse peptides and peptidomimetics reveals shared activities, but with different kinetics, defining two classes with opposite trade-offs. Class I peptides cause abrupt growth arrest coupled with inner-membrane permeabilization and ribosome/DNA reorganization, conferring fast, multipronged action. However, rapid intracellular absorption by the first permeabilized cells depletes the extracellular pool, rendering these peptides ineffective against dense populations, including biofilms. Class II peptides act more gradually, with delayed or absent inner-membrane permeabilization, limiting their speed of action. However, this results in slower intracellular absorption and greater efficacy at high cell densities and against biofilms. These opposing trade-offs point to important immunological and therapeutic implications.

candidates.title: Structural basis for proton-powered secretion by the bacterial flagellar export machinery.
candidates.abstract: Bacterial flagella solve the challenge of moving proteins across the inner membrane without disrupting electrochemical gradients by using a conserved type III secretion system powered by those very gradients. As precise structural and mechanistic details of this process are lacking, we here present single-particle cryo-EM structures at 2.5-4.3 Å resolution of the intact Salmonella enterica flagellar export apparatus, comprising the export gate, FlhB and FlhA. The transmembrane domain of FlhA forms a nonameric funnel, separated from the export gate/FlhB complex above it by an annular lipid layer. Each FlhA subunit harbours a buried pathway of conserved, functionally important hydrophilic residues spanning the hydrophobic core of the membrane. FlhB is observed to wrap around the export gate before threading through the centre of the FlhA channel to the cytoplasm. These structures define the architecture of the proton-transducing element of the type III secretion system, suggesting a rotary gating mechanism with parallels to the FO motor of ATP synthase.

candidates.title: Drought tolerance-enhancing fungal pathogens reprogram plant cell identity through mRNA turnover.
candidates.abstract: The co-occurrence of drought stress and pathogen infections, intensified by climate change, poses a major challenge in plant science. Wilt pathogens that colonize water-conducting plant tissues can aggravate the problem. Whereas Verticillium dahliae infections typically trigger wilt symptoms resulting from xylem occlusion, its relative V. longisporum induces formation of new tracheary elements. This developmental reprogramming associates with altered drought responses. Here, we identify a Verticillium protein, TRANSDIFFERENTIATION EFFECTOR (TRADE), which stimulates conversion of plant cells into tracheary elements. TRADE associates with the plant protein VARICOSE (VCS), a conserved component of the mRNA turnover machinery in plants and metazoans. This is accompanied by SUCROSE NON-FERMENTING 1 (SNF1)-related protein kinase (SRK)-dependent phosphorylation and dysfunction of VCS, altering the abundance of mRNAs regulating xylem differentiation, including WOUND INDUCED DEDIFFERENTIATION 1, a key transcription factor in tissue regeneration. Our findings reveal how a single pathogen effector hijacks cell fate and promotes ectopic xylem formation.

candidates.title: Vagus nerve stimulation ameliorates epilepsy via a gut microbiota-butyrate-vagal axis.
candidates.abstract: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is a therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy, yet its mechanisms are incompletely understood. We demonstrate that VNS modulates the gut microbiome and alters butyrate levels to reduce seizure susceptibility via vagus nerve-dependent signaling. In a longitudinal cohort of patients with epilepsy, VNS enriched short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, including Akkermansia muciniphila, Prevotella, Alistipes, and Odoribacter. Among responders, fecal butyrate decreased concomitantly with increased plasma butyrate concentrations. Fecal microbiota transplantation from post-VNS patients into mice reduced seizure severity and improved gut barrier integrity. In a murine seizure model, VNS similarly increased Akkermansia, while decreasing fecal butyrate levels. A. muciniphila colonization or butyrate supplementation attenuated seizures, effects requiring intact vagal signaling. Knockdown of butyrate receptor GPR41 in the nodose ganglion attenuated the anti-seizure effects of VNS. Our findings illuminate a microbiota-butyrate-vagal pathway mediating VNS efficacy, highlighting the gut-brain axis as a target for epilepsy treatment.

candidates.title: Salinity shapes within- and between-host infection dynamics of the oyster pathogen Vibrio aestuarianus.
candidates.abstract: Environmental variability plays a central role in shaping infectious disease dynamics in marine ecosystems, yet the mechanistic basis of its effects on host-pathogen interactions remains largely unresolved. Recurrent adult mortalities of the Pacific oyster (Magallana gigas) are frequently associated with Vibrio aestuarianus subsp. francensis, but the environmental drivers of outbreak dynamics remain poorly understood. Using complementary approaches spanning national surveillance, field monitoring, controlled experiments, and separate bacterial and host transcriptomic analyses, we assessed distinct aspects of the relationship between salinity and disease dynamics. Twelve years of surveillance data showed that V. aestuarianus was more frequently detected at sites classified as variable-salinity environments, while lower salinity was associated with greater oyster mortality during field monitoring in the Thau Lagoon (France). Under controlled conditions, low salinity increased oyster mortality and enhanced transmission by promoting bacterial shedding, viability and relative dominance in seawater. Transcriptomic analyses showed that low salinity induces the expression of metabolic, stress-response, and virulence-associated genes in V. aestuarianus, while high salinity primarily triggers osmotic stress adaptation. Separate transcriptomic analyses revealed that oyster haemocytes exhibited a salinity-dependent shift. Low salinity is associated with metabolically intensive processes whereas higher salinity conditions are characterized by enrichment of immune-related signalling pathways during infection. Together, these complementary datasets support salinity as an important ecological regulator of V. aestuarianus disease dynamics and identify candidate physiological processes that may contribute to the observed phenotypes. Integrating salinity into disease risk assessment may improve prediction and management of oyster mortality under increasing hydrological variability in coastal environments.

candidates.title: Obesity-associated changes in immune cell dynamics during alphavirus infection revealed by single-cell transcriptomic analysis.
candidates.abstract: Obesity alters host immunity, resulting in worse disease outcomes following infection with various pathogens, including arthritogenic alphaviruses. However, the impact of obesity on the functional landscape of immune cells during acute arthritogenic alphavirus infection remains incompletely explored. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to dissect the blood and tissue immune responses to Mayaro virus (MAYV) infection in lean and obese mice. Footpad injection of MAYV caused significant shifts in immune cell populations and induced robust expression of interferon response and proinflammatory cytokine genes and related pathways in both blood and tissue. In MAYV-infected lean mice, single-cell analysis of the footpad response revealed a unique macrophage subset (F4/80 lo MHCII + ) with high expression of interferon-responsive genes that was replaced by an alternative, F4/80 int population in infected obese mice. Macrophages isolated from lean mice had higher levels of inflammatory gene expression. Furthermore, obese macrophages infected with MAYV and CHIKV ex vivo produce an immunoregulatory response (IL-10) compared to lean macrophages that produce a higher pro-inflammatory response (TNF). The stronger inflammatory response in lean macrophages was associated with less severe systemic disease in lean mice. These results provide evidence for the role of a unique population of macrophages that may contribute to the superior capacity of lean mice to control arthritogenic alphavirus infection.IMPORTANCEArthritogenic alphaviruses-including chikungunya, Mayaro, and Ross River viruses-cause chronic, often disabling joint and muscle disease and are expanding into new regions, yet no approved therapies target the disease process itself. Obesity is a known risk factor for more severe outcomes after infection, but the underlying immune mechanisms have been unclear. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we show that infection drives widespread interferon and inflammatory responses in blood and infected tissue and that obesity specifically alters the macrophage populations present at the infection site. Lean mice mount a highly activated, interferon-driven macrophage response linked to better control of local inflammation, while obese mice instead accumulate a related but less activated population enriched for necroptosis-associated genes and linked to greater tissue damage. These findings identify a specific macrophage subset as a likely contributor to the more severe alphavirus disease seen with obesity and a potential target for future therapies.

candidates.title: Selective suppression and biasing of chemokine receptors CCR9 and ACKR4 through targeting CCL25 with de novo miniproteins.
candidates.abstract: Chemokines and their receptors mediate cell migration and coordinate immune responses, while dysregulation can lead to inflammation. Therapeutic modulation of the chemokine signaling axis has proven difficult. Most drug discovery efforts target the receptors, whereas natural regulatory mechanisms modulate immune responses by directly binding to or modifying the chemokine ligands. Despite this insight, development of effective chemokine-directed modulators has remained elusive. Recent advances in de novo protein design offer an unprecedented opportunity to produce high-affinity binders that efficiently block protein-protein interactions. We implemented a computational workflow leveraging the BindCraft platform to generate miniprotein binders against CCL25, the chemokine ligand for the receptors CCR9 and ACKR4, and implicated in inflammatory bowel diseases. The unbiased development results in several miniproteins designed to block the receptor N-terminus from wrapping the chemokine and preventing productive engagement. Thus, these proteins suppress CCL25-mediated effector coupling and halt MOLT-4 lymphoblast migration. Another class of miniprotein, represented by VUP25111, is predicted to bind CCL25 along the chemokine β1 strand and retained receptor binding. This complex inhibited arrestin recruitment to CCR9, but not to ACKR4, indicating receptor specificity. Additionally, G protein recruitment to CCR9 was unimpeded by VUP25111, suggesting that the miniprotein biased the native agonist towards G proteins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of differentially targeting CCL25 to suppress CCR9 signaling and new tools to resolve the structural basis of chemokine receptor activation and bias.

candidates.title: Developmental bias explains the evolutionary trend towards simple leaf shapes.
candidates.abstract: The relative influence of developmental bias and natural selection on evolutionary outcomes remains a central, unresolved question in evolutionary biology. Here, we combine large-scale phylogenetic trees with herbarium data to confirm that, across the evolutionary history of angiosperms, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes have occurred at a significantly higher rate than the reverse. To investigate whether this directional trend reflects an underlying developmental bias, we simulate evolutionary transitions by introducing random mutations into a well-established computational model of leaf development. Despite excluding selection, the transition rates produced by the model closely align with those observed in the phylogenetic data. This agreement indicates that a strong developmental bias, reflecting the relative ease with which gene regulatory networks generate simple over complex leaves, has played a major role in shaping the evolution of leaf morphology. Our findings echo recent work showing that similar biases towards simplicity influence the evolution of molecular structures, including RNA secondary structures and protein quaternary assemblies. Together, these results suggest that a developmental bias favouring simplicity may be a widespread and general feature of evolutionary systems.

candidates.title: Species diversity increases information flow about predation in bird communities
candidates.abstract: by Agnishikhe Kumar, Jiahao Wu, Ping Ding, Jakob Bro-Jørgensen, Mylène Dutour, Ari E. Martínez, Xingfeng Si, Qiang Zhang, Eben Goodale The Biodiversity-Ecosystem Functioning (BEF) literature has shown species diversity to be essential for ecosystem functioning and services. Yet this concept has not been extended often to behavioral ecology, so that although it is understood that acquiring social information from heterospecific individuals is an important component of ecosystem functioning, it is unclear how animal signaling at the community level, and subsequent information flow, is related to increased species diversity. Eliciting vocal responses using predator models across 10 nature reserves on a latitudinal gradient, we first show that the species diversity of birds is correlated with signaling about predation, both in the low-risk system of mobbing and in the higher-risk system of alarm calls. After finding a similar result across a fragment area gradient in one reserve, we used this system to test how interspecific information flow is affected by species diversity. Potential mechanisms behind this effect include that species are complementary in the characteristics of their mobbing calls, so more species translates into more cumulative information, or there are higher signaling rates as more individuals are involved, or a specific keystone species is more likely to occur. This experiment varied the number of species producing mobbing calls (one, two, four, eight species), with two playback construction methods (standardizing call rate, as typical for BEF experiments, or letting it increase with species richness, as in natural assemblages). Heterospecific mobbing participation (number of vocal species, number of participating individuals), and responses (call rate, probability to call in the first minute and frequency range) increased with species richness. Construction method significantly interacted with species richness, as non-standardized exemplars showed accentuated response as species richness increased. These results match expectations that complementary differences among species in the acoustic characteristics of mobbing calls, and increased call rate, both contribute to the result. There was little evidence that the signals of one particular species changed the experimental result. The overall evidence thus supports the hypothesis that the species diversity of a community is a key component influencing the quantity and the characteristics of signaling and information flow inside it.

candidates.title: Longitudinal analysis of vaccine-associated alterations in the faecal microbiota of layer chickens using a vaccination schedule representative of commercial practice.
candidates.abstract: The gut microbiota is crucial for immune development and overall health in chickens. In commercial production, birds routinely receive multiple vaccines during early life. While individual vaccines are known to affect microbial composition, the impact of complex, multi-vaccine programs, as used in the poultry industry, is not well understood. This pilot longitudinal study examined the impact of multiple live and inactivated vaccines, given at commercially relevant times from an early age, on gut microbial diversity and composition in layer chickens. We characterized microbiota profiles using 16S rRNA gene sequencing at pre- and post-vaccination timepoints across different vaccine groups. Overall, microbial diversity remained stable across most vaccines, indicating strong resilience of the gut microbiota to repeated immunological interventions. Differential abundance analyses didn't identify significant changes in taxa following vaccination. The gut microbial community also showed stability after the completion of the vaccination schedule. These preliminary findings underscore the robustness of the chicken gut ecosystem and lay a foundation for future research into microbiome-vaccine interactions and their implications for poultry health, immunity, and production efficiency.

candidates.title: Species-Specific Responses to Snake Fungal Disease: Effects on Space Use, Detection, and Density in Two Semi-Aquatic Natricine Species.
candidates.abstract: Wildlife diseases pose increasing threats to reptiles, and evaluating the population-level impacts is often challenging due to the cryptic nature and low detectability of many species. Snake Fungal Disease (SFD or ophidiomycosis), caused by the fungal pathogen Ophidiomyces ophidiicola , has emerged as a potential threat to snake populations, yet few studies have documented population declines directly linked to the disease. We utilized 3 years of passive integrated transponder tag telemetry, disease monitoring, and multi-session spatial capture-recapture models to investigate the effects of snake fungal disease on population densities, spatial scale of detection values, and detection probabilities of Common Watersnake ( Nerodia sipedon ) and Queensnake ( Regina septemvittata ) populations in three central Kentucky streams. We hypothesized that SFD would alter population density over time and that SFD-related physiological impairment or behavioral change would result in species-specific changes in space use and detection probability. Density estimates declined across most sites and sessions over the study period, although these declines were generally not statistically significant, and we could not link them to differences in prevalence rates between sites. Infected N. sipedon exhibited significantly smaller spatial scale of detection values compared to non-infected individuals, whereas no significant differences were observed in R. septemvittata . Infection status did not affect the detection probability of either species, but N. sipedon detection probability increased with day of year, and R. septemvittata detection probability increased with rain accumulation between survey periods. These results indicate that SFD may pose an ongoing risk to snake population stability and can produce sublethal, species-specific effects on space use well before potential population declines and highlight the need for long-term monitoring programs that integrate multiple survey methods and emerging technologies to enhance detection probability and population-level inference.

candidates.title: Optimization of the pC-HSL-Induced Transcriptional Regulator, Rpa, for Use in Plant Synthetic Biology.
candidates.abstract: Advancements in plant synthetic biology rely on developing genetic parts with reliable and tunable expression levels for regulation of large genetic pathways. A slow design-build-test cycle and vast design space for modifying genetic parts make precise development of plant synthetic biology tools a challenge. In this work, a transcriptional activator derived from Rhodopseudomonas palustris and re-tooled to function in plants was optimized for low basal expression and high activated expression upon induction with the ligand p-Coumaroyl-homoserine lactone. Modifications to the activation domain, nuclear localization signal, DNA operator design, minimal promoter driving the reporter gene, and combinatorial pairings of these modifications resulted in significant variation in the dynamic range of the system. The overall lowest basal expression produced from the tested designs was approximately 30% that of the internal reference gene elongation factor-1 α and the greatest activated expression produced was approximately 130-fold induction. Functionality of expression from the optimized activation system was demonstrated in both transient Nicotiana benthamiana assays and stably transformed potato, with successful induction observed from a range of concentrations and application methods of p-Coumaroyl-homoserine lactone.

candidates.title: Vaccine chemistry meets avian immune architecture: implications for the breadth and durability of bacterial vaccines in poultry.
candidates.abstract: Formalin inactivation is widely used in poultry bacterins, yet the immunological consequences of formaldehyde-mediated antigen modification remain incompletely defined. Formaldehyde can modify and cross-link proteins and thereby alter proteolytic processing and the peptide repertoire available for major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II) loading. Whether these effects measurably alter bacterial protein-derived MHC-II presentation in chickens, and whether lipopolysaccharide (LPS) structure, accessibility and innate stimulatory activity are preserved under bacterin manufacturing conditions, have not been directly established. We therefore propose a testable framework in which formaldehyde chemistry may differentially affect protein antigen processing and the availability of non-protein innate stimuli. In chickens, this potential imbalance could interact with the distinctive developmental biology of the avian B-cell compartment and influence the breadth and durability of humoral immunity.

candidates.title: Genomic and biological characterization of exopolysaccharides produced by Streptococcus thermophilus CCASU-ST-S3 and CCASU-ST-S52, with statistical optimization and preliminary spectroscopic characterization of EPS-STS3.
candidates.abstract: Background Streptococcus thermophilus is a key dairy starter capable of producing exopolysaccharides (EPS) with strain-dependent biosynthetic and biological properties. Two EPS-producing strains, STS3 and STS52, isolated from yogurt, were characterized genomically, and their partially purified EPS preparations underwent preliminary biological evaluation. Methods Whole-genome sequencing and bioinformatic analyses were used to confirm strain identity, assess safety-associated genomic features, and characterize EPS biosynthetic potential. Partially purified EPS preparations were evaluated for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, cytotoxic effects, wound closure, and antimicrobial activity. EPS production by STS3 was optimized using one-factor-at-a-time screening followed by response surface methodology. The unoptimized EPS-STS3 preparation was separately subjected to preliminary spectroscopic characterization. Results Both strains contained Wzx/Wzy-dependent EPS biosynthetic loci with multiple glycosyltransferase- and Eps-associated genes; STS52 additionally carried a putative pel-like polysaccharide locus. Genome annotation identified nucleotide-sugar precursor pathways. Neither strain harbored acquired antibiotic resistance genes or virulence determinants. EPS-STS3 and EPS-STS52 preparations exhibited 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl radical-scavenging activity (90.1% and 88.9%, respectively) and inhibited albumin denaturation. Both preparations produced dose-dependent reductions in cell viability, with greater effects in Caco-2 cells than WI-38 fibroblasts. The Caco-2 half-maximal inhibitory concentrations were 462.2 and 437.8 µg/mL, respectively. EPS-STS52 produced greater wound closure than EPS-STS3. EPS-STS3 produced promising antibacterial activity against tested Gram-negative bacteria; none was observed for EPS-STS52 or against Gram-positive bacteria or Candida. Optimization raised EPS-STS3 yield to 3.77 g/L (~ 23.56-fold above basal yield) under 3.8% sucrose, 5.8% peptone, pH 5.5, 47 °C, 32 h, and 3% inoculum. The optimized temperature exceeded that commonly reported for S. thermophilus EPS production. Ultraviolet analysis of EPS-STS3 showed no absorbance attributable to proteins or nucleic acids, while Fourier-transform infrared and ¹H/¹³C nuclear magnetic resonance data supported the carbohydrate nature. Conclusion The two locally isolated S. thermophilus strains exhibited distinct EPS biosynthetic features, and their partially purified EPS preparations showed measurable biological activities under the tested conditions. EPS production by STS3 was substantially improved through statistical optimization, while preliminary spectroscopic characterization supported the carbohydrate nature of EPS-STS3. These findings support further structural characterization and biological evaluation of S. thermophilus-derived EPS using more specific and quantitative approaches.

candidates.title: Gut-bacteria-specific CD4 + T cells contribute to HIV persistence during ART.
candidates.abstract: Antigen specificities of most HIV reservoir cells remain poorly defined. We examined whether CD4 + T cells specific for gut bacterial antigens contribute to HIV replication and persistence. Gut-bacteria-specific CD4 + T cells were markedly reduced in viremic people living with HIV (PWH) and remained incompletely restored despite antiretroviral therapy (ART), with those expressing markers of HIV permissiveness being preferentially depleted. Circulating gut-bacteria-specific CD4 + T cells from PWH on ART displayed lower TCR β diversity and persistent functional disruption, characterized by attenuation of canonical effector programs and a higher proportion of cells with cytotoxic features. By contrast, rectum-localized bacteria-specific CD4 + T cells from the same individuals exhibited a tolerogenic profile, highlighting the compartment-specific function of these cells. Near-full-length proviral sequencing revealed clonal expansions of HIV genomes within circulating gut-bacteria-specific CD4 + T cells from ART-treated participants, with evidence of cross-reactivity across multiple bacterial species. Genetically intact proviruses were enriched in Salmonella Typhimurium-specific CD4 + T cells. These findings suggest that gut-bacteria-specific CD4 + T cells are preferentially targeted during untreated HIV infection and incompletely restored by ART, harboring genetically intact HIV genomes and constituting an antigen-driven reservoir in which chronic stimulation by gut microbial antigens promotes clonal proliferation and long-term HIV persistence during ART.

candidates.title: Subacute ruminal acidosis tolerance: phenotyping and nutritional management through host-microbiome interaction insights.
candidates.abstract: Subacute ruminal acidosis (SARA) in dairy cows is commonly assessed through ruminal pH, yet cows differ in the biological consequences of acidogenic challenge. This review frames SARA tolerance as an exposure-adjusted host-microbiome phenotype linking microbial functional stability to biological impairment. It supports future phenotype validation and phenotype-guided nutritional decisions. Oral-rumen microbial connectivity and microbiome-based candidate biomarkers offer translational potential, but standardized phenotypes, longitudinal validation, and prospective feeding trials remain essential.

candidates.title: Effects of long-term exposure to four widely used drinking water regimens on growth performance and fecal microbiota in C57BL/6J mice.
candidates.abstract: Gut microbiota plays a vital role in regulating host physiological status and is susceptible to environmental factors, including different drinking water regimens. This study aimed to explore the effects of long-term exposure to four commonly used drinking water regimens on growth performance and fecal microbiota in C57BL/6J mice. A total of 32 male mice were randomly divided into four groups and continuously administered reverse osmosis water (ROW), hydrochloric acid-acidified water (HCl-AW), sulfuric acid-acidified water (H2SO4-AW), and chlorinated water (CW) for 12 weeks, respectively. Body weight, feed intake, and water intake were measured weekly. After 12 weeks of intervention, fecal samples were collected and subjected to 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing. Bioinformatic analyses were used to characterize microbial community diversity, composition, and predicted functional profiles. The results demonstrated that the ROW group had the highest fecal microbial α-diversity, while the CW group showed the lowest α-diversity. Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on β-diversity revealed clear separation of microbial communities among groups. At the phylum level, significant differences were observed in the relative abundances of Bacteroidota, Firmicutes, Deferribacterota, and Actinobacteriota among all groups. At the genus level, the four drinking water regimens significantly altered the relative abundances of Muribaculaceae, Parabacteroides, Ruminococcaceae, the Eubacterium coprostanoligenes group, Turicibacter, and Bifidobacterium. Functional prediction further revealed significant shifts in multiple microbial metabolic pathways. In terms of growth performance, no significant intergroup differences in body weight or gross weight gain were observed, whereas feed and water intake were markedly altered by different drinking water regimens. In summary, long-term exposure to these four drinking water regimens can profoundly and differentially alter the diversity, composition, and predicted functional profiles of fecal microbiota, and modify feed and water intake in C57BL/6J mice, without inducing significant changes in body weight.

candidates.title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
candidates.abstract: by William R. Milligan, Laura K. Hayward, Guy Sella When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation–selection–drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. Using this model, we delimit how the contributions of large-effect and polygenic changes to adaptation depend on the genetics and ecology of adaptive traits, as well as on other salient factors. Thus, we formulate testable predictions for when different modes of adaptation are expected.

candidates.title: Laxative treatment perturbs gut microbiome composition and metabolism in humans independent of short-term fiber consumption: a randomized controlled crossover intervention study.
candidates.abstract: Gastrointestinal transit time is a major ecological determinant of the human gut microbiome, yet causal evidence that disentangles the effects of diet from those of the gut environment remains limited. Here, we conducted a randomized, controlled crossover trial in healthy adults (nine females, four males) consuming fully standardized high-fiber (40 g/d) or low-fiber (10 g/d) diets to assess how manipulating the gut environment using an osmotic laxative (Movicol) affects gut microbial composition and metabolism. Contrary to our hypothesis, laxative treatment did not affect the saccharolytic-to-proteolytic ratio. Yet, it induced a pronounced microbiome perturbation, explaining 16.3% of the variation in microbial community structure, compared with 1.7% explained by diet. The laxative treatment reduced the absolute abundance of several gram-positive commensals, including butyrate-producing taxa, while increasing gram-negative genera such as Bacteroides , Alistipes , and Phocaeicola . Our findings identify perturbations to the gut environment as a prominent short-term driver of human gut microbiome structure, independent of short-term fiber intake. Together, these results challenge a diet-centric view of microbiome modulation and raise concerns about potential detrimental effects on the gut microbiome in chronic use of gut environment-altering drugs such as macrogol-based laxatives.

[Introduction]
The human gastrointestinal tract harbors a dense and diverse microbial community that has co-evolved with its host in a symbiotic relationship. 1 This ecosystem contributes to digestion, host metabolism, and immune regulation, and disruptions to it have been linked to a wide range of diseases and health outcomes. 2 Dietary changes can alter microbial composition within days, and the microbiota can quickly return toward its previous composition after resumption of the habitual diet. 3 Nevertheless, although diet is a key determinant of microbial composition, providing both substrates and selective pressures, 4 interindividual variation in the gut microbiome cannot be fully explained by diet alone. 5 Large cohort studies consistently show that host-derived abiotic factors, particularly gastrointestinal transit time and pH, explain more of the variation in microbiome composition and metabolism between individuals than dietary patterns. 6-11 Observational and in vitro studies have found that a faster colonic transit time is associated with gut ecosystem maturation and a higher ratio of saccharolytic-to-proteolytic fermentation. 12-14 These findings underscore that the gut microbiota is strongly shaped by the physical environment in which it resides. This has led to the proposal of a conceptual framework in which the gastrointestinal environment defines the ecological boundaries within which microbes persist, diversify, and compete, whereas diet shapes the functional niches within those boundaries, primarily through regulating substrate availability. 15 In this context, controlling diet is essential for isolating the effects of environmental drivers such as intestinal transit time by minimizing variation in substrate supply to the gut microbiota.
Transit time can be manipulated with laxatives (which accelerate transit) and antidiarrheals (which slow down transit). Few randomized controlled trials have investigated the direct effects of manipulating gastrointestinal transit on the gut microbiota, 16-19 largely corroborating the findings from observational and in vitro studies. 9 , 11-13 , 20-22 Stephen et al. (1987) demonstrated that senna-induced acceleration of intestinal transit time increased fecal bacterial dry mass. 16 Lewis and Heaton (1997) reported significant changes in WGTT and fecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations following 9-d interventions with wheat bran, senna, and loperamide, separated by washout periods of at least 14 d. 18 Similar

[Materials and methods]
An open, randomized, controlled trial with a parallel whole-meal intervention (low vs. high-fiber diet) and crossover laxative treatment within each arm to manipulate whole-gut transit time (WGTT) in healthy adults was designed (see Figure 1A). The study was conducted at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise, and Sports at the University of Copenhagen, Denmark, from October 2023 to December 2024. The protocol was approved by the ethics committee of the Capital Region of Denmark (H-23033118), and all participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and a GDPR consent form, as required by Danish law. The study was registered at Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT06022302) in November 2023. This study followed the SAGER guidelines. Biological sex (female/male) was self‑reported and considered in the study design, including eligibility criteria and stratified randomization. The study was not powered to assess sex‑specific effects; therefore, analyses were not stratified by sex.
Of the 22 enrolled participants, 12 completed the entire study (see full flowchart in Figure 1B). The inclusion criteria were (1) age 18–75 y, (2) BMI 18.5–30 kg/m2, (3) self-reported ≤ 3.5 spontaneous bowel movements per week, (4) willingness to collect and temporarily store biological samples at home, (5) willingness to eat the provided foods, and (6) access to a smartphone. Exclusion criteria were (1) pregnant or lactating women, (2) diagnosis of gastrointestinal (GI) disorders (irritable bowel syndrome, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, inflammatory bowel diseases, gastrointestinal obstruction, ischemic colitis), (3) diagnosis of constipation according to the ROME IV criteria, (4) intake of antibiotics <1 month prior to the intervention or any medication that can affect the outcomes of the study, (5) regular use of diarrhea inhibitors or laxatives, dysphagia, any chronic disease that could affect the outcomes of the study or pose a risk when consuming Movicol, (6) intake of medications potentially altering gastric pH (proton pump inhibitors, histamine receptor antagonists, antacids), (7) intake of medications potentially altering the GIT motility (prokinetics, antiemetic agents, anticholinergic agents, narcotic analgesics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and peroral glucocorticoids), (8) concurrent participation in another trial, or any condition that lead the project responsible researcher doubt the feasibility of the volunteer's particip

[Results]
We conducted the randomized, controlled, crossover trial in healthy adults (n = 13, Figure 1A) with a self-reported defecation frequency of fewer than 3.5 bowel movements per week from October 2023 to December 2024. Approximately 400 individuals responded to the recruitment ads. Of those, 22 were randomized to the low-fiber (n = 12) and high-fiber (n = 10) diet arms. Four participants in each arm discontinued before the end of the first period due to personal (n = 5) or unrelated medical reasons (n = 3) (Figure 1B). One participant in the low-fiber diet arm discontinued before completing the second period due to an adverse response to the diet and laxative treatment. No serious adverse events occurred during the trial (see Table S7 for details). Consequently, 12 participants completed both crossover periods. In addition, one participant in the high-fiber arm who discontinued before completing the second period, for reasons unrelated to the study, contributed data from the completed period, and was included in relevant available-case analyses. Thus, the available population comprised up to 13 participants (mean age = 46 y, mean BMI = 24.4 kg/m2, mean WGTT = 53 hours; baseline characteristics in Table 1), depending on the outcome and contrast. Testing the low- and high-fiber groups at baseline indicated even alignment of randomization despite the low sample size (Table 1).
Note: Baseline characteristics of participants in the low‑fiber and high‑fiber diet arms. Values are presented as mean (standard deviation) unless otherwise indicated. Hydrogen and methane were measured in breath exhalations in a fasted state. BMI, body mass index; HbA1c, hemoglobin aAc; LDL, low-density lipoprotein; HDL, high-density lipoprotein.
Body weight, physical activity, alcohol and coffee intake appeared stable during the study (Figure S4 and Table S8). The average energy intake was similar across the baseline phases in the low-fiber diet arm; however, in the high-fiber diet arm, it increased during the second baseline phase, concomitant with a rise in average dietary fiber intake (Figure 1C and D). On average, the low-fiber diet halved, and the high-fiber diet doubled the participants' usual intake of dietary fibers (Figure 1D). All meals provided were consumed, except for two individuals on the high-fiber diet who skipped a few entire meals (4%–6% of the meals provided) due to lack of appetite or forgetting to bring them. [Discussion]
Here, we designed a randomized controlled dietary trial with a nested crossover design to examine the causal effects of WGTT and the interaction between diet and WGTT on the microbiome composition and activity. Based on previous observations, 12 , 13 , 17 , 18 , 21 , 63-65 we hypothesized that a faster WGTT would lead to a shift toward more saccharolytic and less proteolytic fermentation. We furthermore hypothesized that the high-fiber diet would similarly promote this shift compared to baseline, whereas the low-fiber diet would do the opposite. The intervention successfully changed stool consistency and frequency, but did not accelerate WGTT as hypothesized. The main outcome of the study was the fecal butyrate-to-urinary p-cresol sulfate ratio, markers of saccharolytic and proteolytic fermentation, respectively, reflecting shifts in microbial fermentative activity. Contrary to our hypothesis, we did not observe an increase in the butyrate/p-cresol-sulfate ratio following laxative treatment. Instead, we observed a tendency toward decreased propionate in both diet arms, along with decreased acetate and a tendency toward decreased butyrate in the high-fiber diet arm when comparing treatment phases. The same trend was observed across most other microbial metabolic activity markers in both diet arms. Although the laxative treatment did not alter WGTT as hypothesized, it imposed ecological stress on the gut microbiome, impacting metabolic efficiency.
The laxative treatment markedly affected gut microbiome composition by significantly reducing the absolute abundance of genera that accounted for 48% of the average relative abundance under the control treatment, corroborating the trend of a reduced metabolic output. Although we did not observe a reduction in total fecal bacterial cell counts following laxative treatment, previous randomized controlled trials that manipulated intestinal transit time with drugs have reported increases in total bacterial mass and total stool weight following laxative treatment 16 , 18-20 . Therefore, our findings appear to differ from those of others. These previous studies all used the laxative medication senna to induce laxative effects. candidates.title: The gut‒kidney axis.
candidates.abstract: Gut-kidney dialog is integral to the holobiont. This review explores the interactions between these two organ-systems across physicochemical, endocrine, immune, and metabolic levels. It is argued that the gut makes physiological concessions favoring the microbiota, which must be assured by the kidneys, extending the concept of renal homeostasis to holostasis . When considering pathological situations, three dimensions of the gut‒kidney axis are identified: (1) the gut causing kidney disease, (2) the effect of renal failure on the gut, and (3) the systemic effects of the gut in renal failure. Causal roles of the gut in enteric hyperoxaluria, IgA nephropathy and diabetic nephropathy are described. The impact of a uremic environment on the gut is discussed. Conversely the intestinal origins of uremic toxins and their impact on distant organs, including the kidneys themselves, are outlined. Special consideration is given to host-microbiota immune interactions, immunosuppressive therapy and kidney transplantation. Therapeutic interventions targeting the gut-kidney axis are appraised.

[Introduction]
The kidneys filter, sort, and drain waste from the holobiont – an ecosystem encompassing the human body and its microbiota. The gut is a vibrant habitat central to the holobiont. Metabolites generated by the microbiota from food in the gut sustain the host, but can also be harmful. Conversely, if host metabolites fail to be eliminated by the kidneys, they overflow into the gut where they can disrupt microbial communities. 1 , 2
In health, by-products of both host and microbial metabolism reach the kidneys via the circulation, where they are eliminated in the urine. The kidneys collaborate with the gut to ensure circulatory homeostasis by regulating salt and water balance. 3 The mucosal immune system is the host’s chief interlocutor with the gut flora, and perturbation of this relationship leads to inflammation that can have consequences both locally and systemically. 4 , 5 As such, the kidneys are susceptible to up-stream processes in the gut, while in turn, a healthy gut depends on the kidneys to prevent stagnation within the holobiont.
Metabolic, cardiovascular and immune-mediated diseases are major causes of kidney failure. Our understanding of how host‒microbiota interactions in the gut contribute to these processes is advancing. 6
In this review, key concepts concerning the gut‒kidney axis are discussed, and interactions between these two organ-systems are explored across three dimensions: (1) the causal role of the gut in kidney disease, (2) the effect of renal failure on the gut, and (3) the systemic effects of the gut in renal failure (Figure 1).

Green arrows: represent the second dimension, which describes the effect of kidney disease on the gut microbiota, resulting from the influence of a uremic environment on microbial communities. Orange arrow: represents the third dimension, defined by the systemic pathological effects of toxic gut-derived metabolites (uremic toxins) that ordinarily are eliminated by the kidneys, but accumulate in kidney failure; these affect the cardiovascular system, skeleton, erythropoiesis and the kidneys themselves. Over recent decades, we have shifted from viewing the human body through an anthropocentric lens to seeing it as a unique habitat with diverse microbial niches whose inhabitants can influence host health. 58 , 59
The first large, culture-independent insight into the diversity and complexity of the human microbiota was provided by Eckburg et al. in 2005, who analyzed feces and 6 colonic sites across 3 individuals using 16S rRNA sequencing. Differences in microbiota composition were seen to be much greater between individuals than across colonic sites within each individual. 60 Since then, two major groups – the European Metagenomics of the Human Intestinal Tract (MetaHIT) 61 , 62 and the American Human Microbiome Project (HMP) 63–65 – have shone further light on the nature of the human microbiota. The vast majority of microorganisms (>90%) are bacteria, with smaller representation from viruses (5.8%), Archaea (0.8%), and prokaryotes, including yeast and protozoa (0.5%). 62 Among the bacteria, two divisions predominate: Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes. The human intestinal virome is dominated by bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) along with some plant viruses and is composed of <1% eukaryotic viruses. 66 Archaea are represented predominantly by Methanobrevibacter smithii. 60,67 The human mycobiome is represented by species from Saccharomyces, Malassezia, and Candida. 68
Taxonomic analyses tell us which microbial species are present. Functional analyses define metabolic pathways at play and tell us what the microbial community is doing. While there can be significant variability in the species present at different anatomical niches across populations, core metabolic pathways tend to be preserved. These pathways can either be inferred from 16S rRNA data using bioinformatic tools such as PiCRUSt2, or they can be directly observed using metagenomic analyses. 69

To achieve this balance, a single layer of epithelium is supported by a diplomatic mucosal immune system which tempers inflammatory responses that would otherwise compromise the mucosal barrier – commensal microorganisms are tolerated, and microaggressions are dealt with passively. The success of this approach lies in an effective physical barrier that pre-empts conflict and by incapacitating potential pathogens until they are eliminated by peristalsis.
The epithelial surface of the gastrointestinal tract is lined with mucins 120 secreted by goblet cells, keeping microorganisms at arms-length from the epithelium. In humans, a single mucus layer in the small intestine extends to become a double-layer in the colon. 120 Mucins are made up of heavily O-glycosylated glycoproteins that form a gel when hydrated, 120 , 121 and serve as an energy source for mucin-degrading members of the microbiota that have adapted to this specific niche. 122 Most innate pattern recognition receptors, such as TLRs, are strategically positioned away from the apical membrane of the intestinal epithelium to avoid false-alarms. 123
Additionally, an arsenal of antimicrobial proteins (AMPs) is secreted along the digestive tract. These AMPs include α-defensins, β-defensins, cathelicidin (LL-37), calprotectins, C-type lectins (RegIIIalpha), lysosyzme C and secretory phospholipase A2 IIa (sPLA2). 124–126

candidates.title: Environmental microbial exposure as an under-measured exposome domain: Links to host microbiomes, immune regulation, and disease epidemiology.
candidates.abstract: Environmental microbial exposure is an under-measured biological component of the exposome and a plausible determinant of immune-mediated disease patterns. Humans encounter microbial communities and products from soil, air, water, vegetation, animals, food systems, farms, indoor dust, healthcare settings, schools, and urban built environments. These exposures may influence gut, skin, airway, oral, and mucosal microbiomes and thereby alter epithelial barrier function, immune tolerance, inflammatory thresholds, and microbial metabolite production. This structured mechanistic narrative review integrates direct environmental-exposure studies, environment-to-host microbiome studies, host-microbiome mechanistic evidence, and translational frameworks. The clearest convergence occurs in asthma and allergic disease, where early-life farm exposure, endotoxin-rich dust, environmental microbial diversity, innate immune modulation, and epithelial A20 regulation support a coherent exposure-response model. Evidence for inflammatory bowel disease and broader respiratory outcomes is biologically credible but less direct, whereas metabolic and systemic inflammatory outcomes remain largely supported by host-microbiome and metabolite mechanisms rather than direct environmental exposure studies. The review therefore distinguishes evidence maturity and mechanistic proximity rather than treating all disease categories equally. It further positions pollution, urbanization, building design, biodiversity loss, diet, antibiotics, and socioeconomic conditions as active modifiers of microbial exposure and host response. Future studies should integrate direct environmental sampling with body-site microbiome profiling, functional multi-omics, immune and barrier biomarkers, geospatial exposure assessment, source tracking, repeated measures, and explicit causal-inference designs. Environmental microbial exposure should be treated neither as uniformly beneficial nor harmful, but as a measurable, context-dependent exposome domain whose health effects depend on composition, dose, timing, route, co-exposures, and host susceptibility.
